content.title: ESC Guidelines
content.narrative_summary: The Preamble outlines the purpose of the ESC Guidelines to summarise and evaluate available evidence, assist healthcare professionals in management decisions, and emphasises that final patient decisions lie with the responsible clinician in consultation with the patient. It describes the guideline development process by the ESC, including registry data collection, Task Force selection, comprehensive evidence review, critical evaluation of diagnostic and therapeutic procedures, declaration and management of conflicts of interest, endorsement and publication by the ESC Committee for Practice Guidelines (CPG) in the European Heart Journal, and the provision of various implementation tools (pocket versions, slide sets, digital formats). It notes the encouragement of national societies to adopt, translate, and implement the guidelines.

section_headings: 2.1 Why do we need new Guidelines on the diagnosis and management of pulmonary embolism?
content.narrative_summary: The text emphasizes that ESC Guidelines do not override the individual responsibility of health professionals to make accurate decisions, verifying rules and regulations per country at the time of prescription. section_headings: 2.2 What is new in the 2019 Guidelines?
content.narrative_summary: The ESC Guidelines integrate updated knowledge on the optimal diagnosis, assessment, and treatment of patients with pulmonary embolism (PE), incorporating new, objectively validated management strategies and referring to supplementary online data for additional tables, figures, and references. These guidelines focus on acute PE diagnosis and management in adult patients, with cross-reference to consensus documents for deep vein thrombosis, aortic/peripheral vascular diseases, and right ventricular function. Section 2.2 outlines 2019 updates, including: age-adjusted D-dimer cut-offs; guidance on radiation dosage for CTPA and lung scans; clear definitions of haemodynamic instability and high-risk PE; recommendations to assess PE severity, comorbidities, and RV dysfunction; a revised acute-phase treatment section with a dedicated high-risk PE algorithm and preference for NOACs over VKAs in eligible patients; an updated risk-adjusted management algorithm; classification of VTE recurrence risk after three months; discussion of extended anticoagulation indications; and removal of the ‘provoked’/‘unprovoked’ terminology. Additional points include parallel presentation of VTE recurrence and bleeding scores, consideration of reduced-dose apixaban or rivaroxaban after six months, alternative anticoagulation strategies for PE in cancer (edoxaban/rivaroxaban vs LMWH) and pregnancy (dedicated diagnostic algorithm and radiation absorption data), and proposals for integrated long-term care models and new patient follow-up algorithms.

rows.recommendation: Rescue thrombolytic therapy is recommended for patients who deteriorate haemodynamically.
Surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed treatment should be considered as alternatives to rescue thrombolytic therapy for patients who deteriorate haemodynamically.
D-dimer measurement and clinical prediction rules should be considered to rule out PE during pregnancy or the post-partum period.
Further evaluation may be considered for asymptomatic PE survivors at increased risk for CTEPH.

content.narrative_summary: Venous thromboembolism (VTE), presenting as DVT or PE, is the third most frequent acute cardiovascular syndrome after myocardial infarction and stroke. Annual incidence rates for PE range from 39–115 per 100 000 population, with higher rates in older individuals, and are rising over time. PE causes substantial mortality (≤300 000 deaths/year in the US) and health economic burden in Europe (≈€8.5 billion/year).

rows.recommendation: A D-dimer test, using an age-adjusted cut-off or adapted to clinical probability, should be considered as an alternative to the fixed cut-off level.
If a positive proximal CUS is used to confirm PE, risk assessment should be considered to guide management.
V/Q SPECT may be considered for PE diagnosis.
Assessment of the RV by imaging or laboratory biomarkers should be considered, even in the presence of a low PESI or a sPESI of 0.
Validated scores combining clinical, imaging, and laboratory prognostic factors may be considered to further stratify PE severity.
When oral anticoagulation is initiated in a patient with PE who is eligible for a NOAC (apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban, or rivaroxaban), a NOAC is the recommended form of anticoagulant treatment.
Set-up of multidisciplinary teams for management of high-risk and selected cases of intermediate-risk PE should be considered, depending on the resources and expertise available in each hospital.
ECMO may be considered, in combination with surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed treatment, in refractory circulatory collapse or cardiac arrest.
Indefinite treatment with a VKA is recommended for patients with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome.
Extended anticoagulation should be considered for patients with no identifiable risk factor for the index PE event.
Extended anticoagulation should be considered for patients with a persistent risk factor other than antiphospholipid antibody syndrome.
Extended anticoagulation should be considered for patients with a minor transient/reversible risk factor for the index PE event.
A reduced dose of apixaban or rivaroxaban should be considered after the first 6 months.
Edoxaban or rivaroxaban should be considered as an alternative to LMWH, with the exception of patients with gastrointestinal cancer.
Amniotic fluid embolism should be considered in a pregnant or post–partum woman, with unexplained haemodynamic instability or respiratory deterioration, and disseminated intravascular coagulation.
Thrombolysis or surgical embolectomy should be considered for pregnant women with high-risk PE.
NOACs are not recommended during pregnancy or lactation.

content.title: 3.2 Predisposing factors
content.narrative_summary: This page discusses environmental and genetic predisposing factors for venous thromboembolism (VTE), explaining the interaction of permanent (patient-related) and temporary (setting-related) risk factors. It highlights major provoking factors such as trauma, surgery, spinal cord injury, cancer subtypes, and the influence of hormonal therapies—including combined oral contraceptives of different generations, intrauterine devices, progesterone-only pills, and post-menopausal hormone replacement—on VTE risk. It notes infection, transfusion, and erythropoiesis-stimulating agents as triggers, and discusses common cardiovascular risk factors.

content.narrative_summary: The text describes the pathophysiological consequences of pulmonary embolism, including ventilation/perfusion mismatch, right-to-left shunting through a patent foramen ovale leading to hypoxaemia and risk of paradoxical embolization, and alveolar haemorrhage causing haemoptysis and pleuritis. It notes that pulmonary infarction may be mild except in cardiorespiratory disease. Acute RV failure, manifesting as systemic congestion from impaired RV filling or reduced RV output, is identified as critical for clinical severity and outcome in acute PE. High-risk PE is defined by haemodynamic instability, encompassing the clinical presentations detailed in Table 4.

content.narrative_summary: The page describes that high-risk pulmonary embolism (PE) requires emergency diagnostic and therapeutic strategies. It introduces Section 4 on Diagnosis, noting increased use of CT pulmonary angiography for PE detection and the need for safe exclusion strategies in low pre-test probability patients. Section 4.1 outlines the non-specific clinical presentation of acute PE (dyspnoea, chest pain, presyncope/syncope, haemoptysis, haemodynamic instability, syncope, asymptomatic incidental findings) and the role of predisposing factors (VTE history, heart failure) in determining clinical probability. Section 4.2 emphasizes combining symptoms and risk factors for pre-test probability assessment, highlighting both empirical clinical judgement and prediction rules.

section_headings: 4.3 Avoiding overuse of diagnostic tests for pulmonary embolism
4.4.2 D-dimer cut-offs adapted to clinical probability
content.narrative_summary: This section discusses the limitations of relying solely on clinical judgment for suspected pulmonary embolism (PE) and introduces validated prediction rules (revised Geneva, Wells). It emphasizes avoiding unnecessary testing by applying the Pulmonary Embolism Rule-out Criteria (PERC) for low-risk patients. D-dimer testing is reviewed: its high negative predictive value makes it useful to exclude PE in low/intermediate probability cases, though its specificity and positive predictive value are low. Age-adjusted D-dimer cut-offs can improve exclusion rates in older patients without increasing false negatives. The YEARS clinical decision rule tailors D-dimer thresholds to clinical probability, reducing imaging needs. Point-of-care D-dimer assays offer remote applicability but have lower sensitivity than laboratory assays and are recommended only for low-pretest-probability patients. Multidetector CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) is introduced as the imaging modality of choice.

content.narrative_summary: Section 4.7 discusses pulmonary angiography as the former gold standard for diagnosing acute PE, its decline in use in favor of CTPA due to similar accuracy, and procedural risks including 0.5% mortality. Section 4.8 reviews the evaluation of MRA for suspected PE, noting low sensitivity, high rates of inconclusive scans, limited availability, and ongoing trials. Section 4.9 describes the role of echocardiography in detecting RV pressure overload and dysfunction in acute PE, the variable predictive value of different echocardiographic criteria, the potential for misleading findings, and limitations of stand-alone echocardiographic parameters.

content.narrative_summary: Echocardiography is not mandatory for haemodynamically stable patients with suspected pulmonary embolism (PE), though it may aid in differential diagnosis of dyspnoea. In high-risk PE, absence of RV overload signs excludes PE as cause of instability; echocardiography can also detect pericardial tamponade, valvular dysfunction, regional LV dysfunction, aortic dissection, or hypovolaemia. Unambiguous RV overload signs (60/60 sign, McConnell sign, or right-heart thrombi) justify emergency reperfusion if CT is not feasible. Mobile right-heart thrombi are detected by TTE, TOE, or CT and are associated with high mortality. Echocardiography may also detect RV wall thickening or high tricuspid regurgitation peak velocity indicating pressure overload. Compression ultrasonography (CUS) has high sensitivity and specificity for proximal symptomatic DVT; a positive proximal CUS in suspected PE generally warrants anticoagulation without further testing. A four-point CUS exam is used, and incomplete vein compressibility confirms DVT. Meta-analyses report high diagnostic odds; CUS is especially useful when CT is contraindicated and more likely positive in patients with leg symptoms.

content.title: 4.11 Recommendations for diagnosis
content.narrative_summary: This table provides the Class of Recommendation and Level of Evidence for diagnostic strategies in suspected pulmonary embolism, covering scenarios of haemodynamic stability, clinical evaluation, D-dimer testing, CTPA, and V/Q scintigraphy.

rows.recommendation: In suspected high-risk PE, as indicated by the presence of haemodynamic instability, bedside echocardiography or emergency CTPA (depending on availability and clinical circumstances) is recommended for diagnosis.
It is recommended that i.v. anticoagulation with UFH, including a weight-adjusted bolus injection, be initiated without delay in patients with suspected high-risk PE.
The use of validated criteria for diagnosing PE is recommended.
Initiation of anticoagulation is recommended without delay in patients with high or intermediate clinical probability of PE while diagnostic workup is in progress.
It is recommended that the diagnostic strategy be based on clinical probability, assessed either by clinical judgement or by a validated prediction rule.

Plasma D-dimer measurement, preferably using a highly sensitive assay, is recommended in outpatients/emergency department patients with low or intermediate clinical probability, or those that are PE-unlikely, to reduce the need for unnecessary imaging and irradiation.

As an alternative to the fixed D-dimer cut-off, a negative D-dimer test using an age-adjusted cut-off (age × 10 μg/L, in patients aged >50 years) should be considered for excluding PE in patients with low or intermediate clinical probability, or those that are PE-unlikely.
As an alternative to the fixed or age-adjusted D-dimer cut-off, D-dimer levels adapted to clinical probability should be considered to exclude PE.
D-dimer measurement is not recommended in patients with high clinical probability, as a normal result does not safely exclude PE, even when using a highly sensitive assay.
It is recommended to reject the diagnosis of PE (without further testing) if CTPA is normal in a patient with low or intermediate clinical probability, or who is PE-unlikely.
It is recommended to accept the diagnosis of PE (without further testing) if CTPA shows a segmental or more proximal filling defect in a patient with intermediate or high clinical probability.
It should be considered to reject the diagnosis of PE (without further testing) if CTPA is normal in a patient with high clinical probability or who is PE-likely.
Further imaging tests to confirm PE may be considered in cases of isolated subsegmental filling defects.
CT venography is not recommended as an adjunct to CTPA.
It is recommended to reject the diagnosis of PE (without further testing) if the perfusion lung scan is normal.
It should be considered to accept that the diagnosis of PE (without further testing) if the V/Q scan yields high probability for PE.
A non-diagnostic V/Q scan should be considered as exclusion of PE when combined with a negative proximal CUS in patients with low clinical probability, or who are PE-unlikely.

content.narrative_summary: This page discusses the prognostic utility of computed tomographic pulmonary angiography (CTPA) parameters—particularly RV enlargement (RV end-diastolic diameter and RV/LV ratio ≥0.9)—as independent predictors of adverse in-hospital and long-term outcomes in patients with acute PE. It highlights meta-analyses linking elevated RV/LV ratios (>1.0) with increased all-cause mortality and the potential value of CT volumetric measures and contrast reflux assessment. In the laboratory biomarkers section, it reviews elevated troponin I/T concentrations on admission and high-sensitivity assays as markers of worse prognosis, the limited specificity of troponins alone, and their additive value when combined with imaging. It then covers markers of RV dysfunction (BNP and NT-proBNP) for risk stratification, including suggested cutoff values (<14 pg/mL for troponin T, <500 pg/mL for NT-proBNP and possibly >600 pg/mL for adverse event prediction), and other biomarkers (lactate, creatinine, neutrophil gelatinase–associated lipocalin, hyponatraemia, and copeptin levels ≥24 pmol/L) associated with PE-related complications and mortality.

section_headings: 5.4 Combined parameters and scores for assessment of pulmonary embolism severity
5.5 Integration of aggravating conditions and comorbidity into risk assessment of acute pulmonary embolism
content.narrative_summary: Section 5.4 describes the use of combinations of clinical, imaging, and laboratory parameters to build prognostic scores (e.g., Bova, H-FABP, Syncope, FAST) for a semi-quantitative assessment of early PE-related death risk, noting that only the combination of RV dysfunction on echocardiogram (or CTPA) with positive cardiac troponin has been tested to guide therapy in a randomized controlled trial. Section 5.5 discusses the incorporation of baseline comorbidities into risk assessment using the Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index (PESI) and its simplified version (sPESI), highlighting their validation for identifying low-risk patients for 30-day mortality and reporting that concomitant DVT is an adverse prognostic factor for 30-day all-cause mortality.

content.narrative_summary: This page discusses further risk stratification of pulmonary embolism (PE) in patients without haemodynamic instability, recommending use of clinical, imaging, and laboratory parameters to distinguish intermediate- and low-risk PE for decisions on early discharge versus hospitalization. It describes high-risk PE as requiring immediate reperfusion and that biomarker testing is not necessary for these patients. The text highlights the PESI and sPESI scores as validated predictors of low-risk PE, classifies intermediate-risk patients with right ventricular dysfunction and elevated biomarkers into intermediate-high risk, and recommends close monitoring (section 7). Alternative prognostic scores and meta-analysis data are noted, with a caution to classify patients with RV dysfunction or elevated troponin as intermediate-low risk despite low PESI or sPESI scores.

section_headings: 6.1.2 Pharmacological treatment of acute right ventricular failure
content.narrative_summary: Section 6.1.1 discusses oxygen therapy and ventilation in severe pulmonary embolism: hypoxaemia due to ventilation–perfusion mismatch, indications for supplemental oxygen when SaO₂ <90%, the role of high-flow nasal cannula and mechanical ventilation, and cautious use of intubation to avoid haemodynamic compromise. Section 6.1.2 reviews pharmacological management of acute right ventricular failure: limited fluid challenge if central venous pressure is low, avoidance of aggressive volume loading, assessment of venous pressure by IVC imaging or monitoring, and the judicious use of vasopressors (e.g., norepinephrine) and inotropes (e.g., dobutamine) depending on haemodynamics.

rows.recommendation: Initial risk stratification of suspected or confirmed PE, based on the presence of haemodynamic instability, is recommended to identify patients at high risk of early mortality.
In patients without haemodynamic instability, further stratification of patients with acute PE into intermediate- and low-risk categories is recommended.

In patients without haemodynamic instability, use of clinical prediction rules integrating PE severity and comorbidity, preferably the PESI or sPESI, should be considered for risk assessment in the acute phase of PE.
Assessment of the RV by imaging methodsc or laboratory biomarkersd should be considered, even in the presence of a low PESI or a negative sPESI.

In patients without haemodynamic instability, use of validated scores combining clinical, imaging, and laboratory PE-related prognostic factors may be considered to further stratify the severity of the acute PE episode.

section_headings: 6.1.4 Advanced life support in cardiac arrest
content.narrative_summary: The text following Table 9 discusses that levosimendan may improve RV–pulmonary arterial coupling by vasodilation and increased contractility, but clinical benefit is unproven. Vasodilators reduce PAP and PVR but risk hypotension; inhaled nitric oxide may help haemodynamics but lacks evidence. Section 6.1.3 outlines mechanical cardiopulmonary support (veno-arterial ECMO) in high-risk PE, noting high complication rates, lack of RCTs, and reports of Impella use. Section 6.1.4 reviews advanced life support in PE-related cardiac arrest, advising adherence to cardiac arrest guidelines and consideration of thrombolytic therapy. Section 6.2 and 6.2.1 describe initial anticoagulation strategies, preferring LMWH or fondaparinux over UFH in PE, with renal impairment dosing considerations.

content.narrative_summary: Non-vitamin K antagonist oral anticoagulants (NOACs) are small molecules directly inhibiting thrombin (dabigatran) or factor Xa (apixaban, edoxaban, rivaroxaban), administered at fixed doses without routine laboratory monitoring. Phase III trials in acute VTE demonstrated non-inferiority to LMWH+VKA and lower major and intracranial bleeding rates, with dose adjustments or exclusions in patients with moderate to severe renal dysfunction. Vitamin K antagonists remain the standard for long-term oral anticoagulation, initiated with parenteral agents until an INR of 2.0–3.0 is achieved, with dosing tailored by age and INR monitoring; pharmacogenetic testing may improve dose precision. Structured anticoagulation services and patient self-monitoring of VKAs can increase time in therapeutic range but have not reduced thromboembolic events. Systemic thrombolysis in pulmonary embolism accelerates improvement in pulmonary obstruction and RV function if given within 48 hours of symptom onset (or up to 6–14 days), but is associated with increased major and intracranial bleeding; meta-analyses and the PEITHO trial support mortality reduction in high- and intermediate-risk PE. Recombinant tissue-type plasminogen activator (rtPA) 100 mg over 2 hours is preferred, though reduced-dose regimens and newer agents (reteplase, desmoteplase, tenecteplase) require further validation. The impact of early thrombolysis on long-term functional outcomes remains unclear.

content.title: 8.5 Management of pulmonary embolism in patients with cancer
section_headings: 8.5 Management of pulmonary embolism in patients with cancer
content.narrative_summary: This section reviews management of pulmonary embolism (PE) in patients with cancer. Low-molecular-weight heparins (LMWH) reduce recurrent venous thromboembolism (VTE) by about 40% compared with vitamin K antagonists (VKAs), with similar bleeding risk, and have become standard despite higher cost. Novel oral anticoagulants (NOACs) offer convenience but have limited data; edoxaban was non-inferior to dalteparin for preventing recurrence, though gastrointestinal bleeding was higher in some cancer patients. Extended anticoagulation beyond 3–6 months should be individualized based on recurrence risk (using a validated cancer-associated VTE score), bleeding risk, patient preference, and response to anticancer therapy; indefinite anticoagulation may be reasonable in those at high risk. Inferior vena cava filters are reserved for contraindications to anticoagulation, not as adjuncts. Diagnostic screening for occult cancer after unprovoked VTE should be limited to history, physical exam, basic labs, and chest X-ray. Incidental PE in cancer patients should be managed similarly to symptomatic PE, regardless of location or extent.

content.narrative_summary: Section 9 discusses the epidemiology and risk factors of pulmonary embolism in pregnancy, highlighting that acute PE remains a leading cause of maternal death, with higher VTE risk during and after pregnancy. Additional risk factors include in vitro fertilization, prior VTE, obesity, comorbidities, stillbirth, pre-eclampsia, postpartum hemorrhage, and caesarean section. Documented risk assessment is essential. Diagnosis is challenging due to overlapping symptoms and rising D-dimer levels; diagnostic algorithms incorporating clinical probability scores, D-dimer measurement, compression ultrasound, and CTPA/single-photon scintigraphy can safely exclude PE in selected women. Imaging tests are guided by a proposed algorithm (Figure 7) with modern techniques minimizing maternal and fetal radiation exposure.

section_headings: 9.3 Treatment of pulmonary embolism in pregnancy
content.narrative_summary: Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) use in pregnancy is limited by unknown long-term fetal effects of gadolinium and frequent nondiagnostic images; conventional pulmonary angiography entails higher fetal radiation and is avoided. Overdiagnosis of PE in pregnancy has significant implications, including bleeding risk and need for thromboprophylaxis in future pregnancies. Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) is the preferred treatment for PE during pregnancy due to predictable pharmacokinetics, placental safety, and favorable risk profile; unfractionated heparin (UFH) has a role in certain high-risk scenarios. Management of labour in anticoagulated women requires multidisciplinary planning, timing of neuraxial anaesthesia relative to the last LMWH dose, and careful postpartum LMWH reinitiation. Anticoagulation should continue for at least 6 weeks postpartum with a minimum total treatment duration of 3 months; LMWH and warfarin are compatible with breastfeeding, whereas NOACs are not recommended.

content.title: 10 Long-term sequelae of pulmonary embolism
section_headings: 10.1 Persisting symptoms and functional limitation after pulmonary embolism
content.narrative_summary: This section reviews long-term outcomes after acute pulmonary embolism (PE). Most survivors have restored pulmonary arterial patency within months, but some develop persistent thrombi and chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH). Follow-up aims include exercise rehabilitation, comorbidity management, behavioural education, and early detection of CTEPH. Cohort studies show 6–36 months post-PE, 20–75% of patients report persisting dyspnoea and reduced physical performance, with predictors including age, comorbidities, higher BMI, elevated pulmonary pressures, and deconditioning. CTEPH incidence after PE ranges from 0.1% to 9.1% in 2 years, with prospective screening strategies involving imaging and hemodynamic assessment. CTEPH pathophysiology involves organized thrombi and microvascular remodelling leading to progressive pulmonary vascular resistance. Predisposing factors include thrombophilic disorders, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, elevated factor VIII, cancer, splenectomy, inflammatory bowel disease, right-to-left shunts, and chronic indwelling lines or devices.

continuity.reason: Section continues beyond this page

content.narrative_summary: Diagnosing CTEPH is challenging due to limited specificity of predictive algorithms, with a median age at diagnosis of 63 years and equal sex distribution. Early CTEPH may lack specific signs, and right heart failure often appears only in advanced disease, leading to a median diagnostic delay of 14 months. Diagnosis requires at least 3 months of effective anticoagulation, mean PAP ≥25 mmHg with pulmonary arterial wedge pressure ≤15 mmHg at right heart catheterization, and demonstration of mismatched perfusion defects on V/Q scan or specific features on CTPA or pulmonary cineangiography. Some patients have normal resting haemodynamics but persistent exercise limitation (CTED). Planar V/Q lung scanning remains the first-line imaging modality (96–97% sensitivity, 90–95% specificity); SPECT is less sensitive. CTPA is useful but not standalone; newer techniques such as dual-energy CT, cone-beam CT, magnetic resonance imaging (inferior to CT), angioscopy, intravascular ultrasound and optical coherence tomography aid lesion characterization. High-resolution CT helps differential diagnosis by identifying emphysema, interstitial lung disease, infarcts and vascular/bronchial malformations; perfusion mosaic patterns are common. Differential diagnoses include pulmonary arteritis, angiosarcoma, tumour embolism, parasitic cysts, foreign body emboli and pulmonary artery stenoses.

figures_tables_algorithms.summary: Two-column table listing findings related to the acute PE event at diagnosis and concomitant chronic diseases and conditions predisposing to CTEPH at diagnosis or 3–6-month follow-up. Findings related to acute PE event include: previous episodes of PE or DVT; large pulmonary arterial thrombi on CTPA; echocardiographic signs of PH/RV dysfunction; and CTPA findings suggestive of pre-existing chronic thromboembolic disease. Concomitant chronic conditions include: ventriculo-atrial shunts; infected chronic i.v. lines or pacemakers; history of splenectomy; thrombophilic disorders (particularly antiphospholipid antibody syndrome and high coagulation factor VIII levels); non-O blood group; hypothyroidism treated with thyroid hormones; history of cancer; myeloproliferative disorders; inflammatory bowel disease; and chronic osteomyelitis.

Chronic treatment and prevention of recurrence
content.narrative_summary: Left column continues a numbered list of management considerations for acute pulmonary embolism (PE), including prompt anticoagulation, use of validated diagnostic algorithms, interpretation of CTPA findings, risk stratification, choice of reperfusion strategies, long-term anticoagulation selection, follow-up imaging, and special situations such as pregnancy and chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH). Right column introduces Section 13 “Gaps in the evidence,” outlining key areas needing further research: optimal D-dimer thresholds and imaging strategies; significance of isolated subsegmental defects; management of incidental PE; evaluation of “triple-rule-out” CT strategies; and evidence gaps in assessing severity, treatment modalities (e.g., reduced-dose thrombolysis, ECMO), anticoagulant regimens in renal impairment, early discharge criteria, and chronic prevention models.

section_headings: 14 'What to do' and 'what not to do' messages from the Guidelines
content.narrative_summary: Further studies are needed on the efficacy and safety of NOACs for treating PE in cancer patients, including clarification of anticoagulant regimens and timing for discontinuation; diagnostic algorithms and optimal LMWH dosing in pregnancy require prospective validation and any fetal exposure to NOACs should be recorded; and follow-up strategies for persistent symptoms and criteria to identify patients at risk of CTEPH need to be defined and validated in cohort studies.

recommendation_tables.title: What to do messages from the Guidelines

rows.recommendation: In suspected high-risk PE, perform bedside echocardiography or emergency CTPA (depending on availability and clinical circumstances) for diagnosis.
In suspected high-risk PE, initiate intravenous anticoagulation with UFH without delay, including a weight-adjusted bolus injection.
In suspected PE without haemodynamic instability, use validated diagnostic criteria.
In suspected PE without haemodynamic instability, initiate anticoagulation in case of high or intermediate clinical probability, while diagnostic workup is in progress.
Base the diagnostic strategy on clinical probability, using either clinical judgement or a validated prediction rule.
Measure D-dimers in plasma, preferably with a highly sensitive assay, in outpatients/emergency department patients with low or intermediate clinical probability, or who are PE-unlikely.
Reject the diagnosis of PE (without further testing) if CTPA is normal in a patient with low or intermediate clinical probability, or if the patient is PE-unlikely.
Reject the diagnosis of PE (without further testing) if the perfusion lung scan is normal.
Accept the diagnosis of PE if CTPA shows a segmental or more proximal filling defect in a patient with intermediate or high clinical probability.
Accept the diagnosis of VTE if CUS shows a proximal DVT in a patient with clinical suspicion of PE.
Do not measure D-dimers in patients with high clinical probability, as a normal result does not safely exclude PE.
Do not perform CT venography as an adjunct to CTPA.
Do not perform MRA to rule out PE.
Stratify patients with suspected or confirmed PE, based on the presence of haemodynamic instability, to identify those at high risk of early mortality.
In patients without haemodynamic instability, further stratify PE into intermediate- and low-risk categories.
Administer systemic thrombolytic therapy to patients with high-risk PE.
Surgical pulmonary embolectomy for patients with high-risk PE, in whom recommended thrombolysis is contraindicated or has failed.
If anticoagulation is initiated parenterally in a patient without haemodynamic instability, prefer LMWH or fondaparinux over UFH.

section_headings: Chronic treatment and prevention of recurrence

rows.recommendation: When oral anticoagulation is initiated in a patient with PE who is eligible for a NOAC (apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban, or rivaroxaban), prefer a NOAC.
As an alternative to a NOAC, administer a VKA, overlapping with parenteral anticoagulation until an INR of 2.5 (range 2.0–3.0) has been reached.
Administer rescue thrombolytic therapy to a patient with haemodynamic deterioration on anticoagulation treatment.
Do not use NOACs in patients with severe renal impairment or in those with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome.
Do not routinely administer systemic thrombolysis as primary treatment in patients with intermediate- or low-risk PE.
Do not routinely use inferior vena cava filters.
Administer therapeutic anticoagulation for ≥3 months to all patients with PE.
Discontinue therapeutic oral anticoagulation after 3 months in patients with first PE secondary to a major transient/reversible risk factor.

Continue oral anticoagulant treatment indefinitely in patients presenting with recurrent VTE (at least one previous episode of PE or DVT) that is not related to a major transient or reversible risk factor.
Continue oral anticoagulant treatment with a VKA indefinitely in patients with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome.
In patients who receive extended anticoagulation, reassess drug tolerance and adherence, hepatic and renal function, and the bleeding risk at regular intervals.
Perform formal diagnostic assessment with validated methods if PE is suspected during pregnancy or in the post-partum period.
Administer therapeutic, fixed doses of LMWH, based on early pregnancy weight, in the majority of pregnant women without haemodynamic instability.
Do not insert a spinal or epidural needle within 24 h since the last LMWH dose.
Do not administer LMWH within 4 h of removal of an epidural catheter.
Do not use NOACs during pregnancy or lactation.
Routinely re-evaluate patients 3–6 months after acute PE.
Implement an integrated model of care after acute PE, in order to ensure optimal transition from hospital to ambulatory care.

Refer symptomatic patients with mismatched perfusion defects on V/Q lung scan beyond 3 months after acute PE to a pulmonary hypertension/CTEPH expert centre, taking into account the results of echocardiography, natriuretic peptide, and/or cardiopulmonary exercise testing.
